questions.stem:
A microbiology student grows Streptococcus pyogenes in broth and adds penicillin G during active growth. Under the microscope over the next hours, the cocci swell and then burst. Analysis of the cell wall material collected just before lysis shows long glycan strands with stem peptides that are not linked to the peptides of neighboring strands. When the same experiment is repeated with cells that are not dividing, lysis is much slower.

Which enzymatic step did the drug most directly block?
choices: Transpeptidation by penicillin-binding proteins that cross-link peptides
Transglycosylation after the drug coats the D-alanyl-D-alanine end of the precursor
Insertion of the drug into the cytoplasmic membrane with loss of membrane potential
Binding of the 30S ribosomal subunit that causes misreading of messenger RNA
Synthesis of the folate cofactors needed to build nucleotides for new DNA strands

explain.html:
Uncross-linked stem peptides are the fingerprint of a beta-lactam. The beta-lactam ring binds the transpeptidase active site of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), the enzymes that cross-link the peptide side chains of peptidoglycan. Without cross-links the wall is weak, autolytic enzymes open lesions in it, and the growing cell lyses. That is why beta-lactams are bactericidal and work best on actively growing cells that are building new wall.

Vancomycin also stops cell wall synthesis, but it does so by binding the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of the precursor, not the PBP. Daptomycin acts on the membrane, aminoglycosides on the 30S subunit and sulfonamides on folate synthesis, so none of them leaves this specific wall defect.
why: Coating the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus is the vancomycin mechanism; vancomycin does not bind PBPs.
Calcium-dependent membrane insertion and depolarization is the daptomycin mechanism.
30S binding with misreading is how aminoglycosides act; it would not leave uncross-linked wall strands.
Folate synthesis is blocked by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, not by penicillin.
explain.takeaway: Beta-lactams bind the transpeptidase domain of penicillin-binding proteins, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and causing lysis of growing bacteria.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 17-year-old girl has 5 days of fever, severe sore throat and fatigue. Examination shows tonsillar exudates, enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes and a palpable spleen tip. A rapid strep test was not done, and she is given an oral antibiotic for presumed bacterial pharyngitis. Two days later she develops a widespread, itchy maculopapular rash over the trunk and limbs. She has taken penicillin V in the past without any reaction.

Which antibiotic was she most likely prescribed?
choices: Cephalexin
Clindamycin
Azithromycin
Amoxicillin
Doxycycline

explain.html:
Exudative pharyngitis with posterior cervical nodes and splenomegaly in a teenager suggests a viral illness, infectious mononucleosis, rather than strep throat. The lecture lists rash with ampicillin or amoxicillin, especially in the setting of a viral illness such as mononucleosis, as a specific adverse event of the aminopenicillins.

She tolerated penicillin V before, which argues that this rash is the aminopenicillin-viral illness interaction and not a true penicillin allergy. Amoxicillin is an expected choice for pharyngitis, which is how this mistake happens in practice.
why: Cephalexin is described as well tolerated with mild GI upset.
Clindamycin's main adverse effects are GI upset and C. difficile colitis, not this rash pattern.
Azithromycin is linked to GI upset and QT prolongation, not the mononucleosis rash.
Doxycycline causes photosensitivity and esophagitis and is not a pharyngitis choice here.
explain.takeaway: Ampicillin and amoxicillin commonly cause a maculopapular rash when given during a viral illness, especially infectious mononucleosis.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old woman is bitten on the hand by her dog. The wound becomes red, warm and swollen over 24 hours. Bite wounds carry a mix of skin and oral flora, including beta-lactamase-producing Staphylococcus aureus and anaerobes. Her physician chooses an oral regimen that pairs amoxicillin with a second compound that has almost no antibacterial activity on its own.

How does the second compound widen the coverage of amoxicillin?
choices: It binds penicillin-binding protein 2a so that amoxicillin can reach the transpeptidase
It inhibits renal dehydropeptidase so that amoxicillin is not inactivated in the kidney
It irreversibly binds bacterial beta-lactamases so they can no longer hydrolyze the amoxicillin
It chelates iron so amoxicillin enters through the bacterial iron transport channels
It blocks bacterial efflux pumps so that amoxicillin builds up inside the periplasm

explain.html:
The regimen is amoxicillin-clavulanate, which the lecture lists for animal bites. Clavulanate is a beta-lactamase inhibitor: it irreversibly binds the beta-lactamases made by bacteria, protecting the partner beta-lactam so it can reach its PBP target.

The result is the take-home rule from the lecture: adding clavulanate, sulbactam or tazobactam extends coverage to beta-lactamase-producing S. aureus (MSSA), more Gram-negatives and anaerobes. The inhibitor does nothing for MRSA, whose resistance is an altered target rather than an enzyme.
why: Binding PBP2a is the property of ceftaroline; beta-lactamase inhibitors do not fix MRSA.
Blocking renal dehydropeptidase is what cilastatin does for imipenem.
Using iron transport channels is the siderophore strategy of cefiderocol.
Efflux pump inhibitors are not part of this combination.
explain.takeaway: Beta-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam) irreversibly bind beta-lactamases, extending the partner beta-lactam to MSSA, more Gram-negatives and anaerobes, as in amoxicillin-clavulanate for animal bites.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 62-year-old man in the intensive care unit develops pneumonia on day 9 of mechanical ventilation. Sputum culture grows an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod with a grape-like odor and a blue-green pigment. The team wants a third-generation cephalosporin that will cover this organism.

Which choice and reasoning are most appropriate?
choices: Ceftriaxone, because it has the strongest Gram-negative activity among third-generation agents
Ceftazidime, because unlike ceftriaxone it has activity against this organism
Cefazolin, because first-generation agents cover the PEcK Gram-negative rods
Ceftaroline, because it binds altered penicillin-binding proteins in Gram-negatives
Cefoxitin, because second-generation agents add anaerobic and hospital Gram-negative coverage

explain.html:
The organism is Pseudomonas aeruginosa: oxidase positive, non-lactose fermenting, grape odor, blue-green pigment, a classic cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia. Among third-generation cephalosporins, the lecture draws a sharp line: ceftriaxone has reliable Gram-positive activity and no Pseudomonas coverage, while ceftazidime has unreliable Gram-positive activity but does cover Pseudomonas.

The other cephalosporins listed do not help: cefazolin covers PEcK organisms, cefoxitin adds anaerobes, and ceftaroline adds MRSA but specifically excludes Pseudomonas. Among other generations, cefepime (fourth) is the anti-pseudomonal workhorse.
why: Ceftriaxone has no Pseudomonas activity, so it would fail here.
First-generation cephalosporins cover Proteus, E. coli and Klebsiella, not Pseudomonas.
Ceftaroline binds PBP2a of MRSA and excludes Pseudomonas.
Cefoxitin adds anaerobes but has no anti-pseudomonal activity.
explain.takeaway: Ceftriaxone is reliable against Gram-positives but lacks Pseudomonas activity, whereas ceftazidime covers Pseudomonas with unreliable Gram-positive activity.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 49-year-old man has right-sided endocarditis. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are resistant to oxacillin, cefazolin and meropenem. A molecular test shows the isolate carries a gene for an altered penicillin-binding protein. The infectious diseases team chooses a cephalosporin rather than a glycopeptide for definitive therapy.

Which property explains why the chosen cephalosporin works when the others failed?
choices: It is resistant to hydrolysis by beta-lactamases made by the staphylococcus
It enters through iron transport channels and bypasses the bacterial outer membrane
It binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus instead of any penicillin-binding protein
It binds the altered penicillin-binding protein that other beta-lactams cannot
It is combined with a beta-lactamase inhibitor that restores its staphylococcal activity

explain.html:
Oxacillin-resistant S. aureus is MRSA. Its resistance comes from an altered target, PBP2a, which does not bind ordinary beta-lactams, so penicillins, cephalosporins and carbapenems all fail. Ceftaroline, the fifth-generation cephalosporin, is the exception the lecture highlights: it binds PBP2a, and it is used for MRSA bacteremia, endocarditis and complicated infections.

Because the problem is the target and not an enzyme, beta-lactamase stability or a beta-lactamase inhibitor does not help. Binding D-Ala-D-Ala is vancomycin, a glycopeptide, which the team chose not to use here.
why: Beta-lactamase stability does not overcome an altered PBP, which is the MRSA mechanism.
The iron transport "Trojan horse" is cefiderocol, a Gram-negative agent.
D-Ala-D-Ala binding is vancomycin, a glycopeptide, not a cephalosporin.
Beta-lactamase inhibitors do not restore activity against MRSA.
explain.takeaway: Ceftaroline is the cephalosporin active against MRSA because it binds PBP2a, the altered penicillin-binding protein.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with a urinary catheter develops sepsis. Blood cultures grow Escherichia coli. Susceptibility testing shows resistance to ampicillin, piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftriaxone, cefepime and aztreonam, and the lab reports the isolate as an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producer. The team picks the beta-lactam class that the lecture calls the drug of choice for severe ESBL infections, and selects the agent in that class that must be co-administered with a second compound.

What does the second compound do?
choices: It inhibits the ESBL enzyme so that the carbapenem ring stays intact
It slows tubular secretion so that the drug can be dosed only once daily
It prevents the drug from binding plasma albumin, raising its free fraction
It protects the drug from destruction by hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes
It blocks renal dehydropeptidase, which would otherwise inactivate the drug

explain.html:
Carbapenems are structurally stable against ESBLs, and the lecture names them the drug of choice for severe infections caused by ESBL-producing organisms. The agent that is always given with a partner is imipenem, paired with cilastatin.

Cilastatin is not an antibiotic and not a beta-lactamase inhibitor. It blocks renal dehydropeptidase, which would otherwise inactivate imipenem in the kidney. Once-daily dosing belongs to ertapenem, which also lacks Pseudomonas coverage.
why: Carbapenems resist ESBLs on their own; cilastatin is not a beta-lactamase inhibitor.
Once-daily dosing is an ertapenem feature, not the role of cilastatin.
Cilastatin does not change albumin binding; poor outcomes with low albumin are an ertapenem issue.
Imipenem is not destroyed by hepatic cytochrome enzymes.
explain.takeaway: Carbapenems are the drug of choice for severe ESBL infections; imipenem is always given with cilastatin, which blocks renal dehydropeptidase inactivation.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old woman who injects drugs has MRSA bacteremia with tricuspid valve endocarditis and is treated successfully with a bactericidal drug that inserts into the bacterial membrane in a calcium-dependent way and depolarizes it. Weekly creatine kinase levels are checked during therapy. Months later she is admitted with MRSA pneumonia, and a student suggests using the same drug again because it worked so well.

Why is that drug a poor choice for her pneumonia?
choices: Pneumococcal surfactant enzymes hydrolyze the drug's beta-lactam ring
It is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and fails in the lung
MRSA becomes resistant to it after one course by making PBP2a
It cannot cross the alveolar capillary barrier because it is too large
It is bacteriostatic in the lung and needs a cell wall agent for synergy

explain.html:
Calcium-dependent membrane insertion with rapid depolarization is daptomycin, a lipopeptide that kills MRSA and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus and is used for endocarditis, bacteremia, skin and bone infections. Creatine kinase is monitored because it can cause myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

The lecture's key restriction is that daptomycin must not be used for pneumonia: lung surfactant inactivates it. For MRSA pneumonia, vancomycin (or linezolid, taught in the next lecture) is used instead.
why: Daptomycin is not a beta-lactam, and surfactant inactivation is not ring hydrolysis.
PBP2a confers beta-lactam resistance and does not affect a membrane-acting drug.
Distribution size is not the reason; surfactant inactivation is.
Daptomycin is bactericidal; synergy with cell wall agents is an aminoglycoside concept.
explain.takeaway: Daptomycin, a calcium-dependent membrane-depolarizing lipopeptide active against MRSA and VRE, is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and is not used for pneumonia; monitor creatine kinase.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old man with a seizure disorder has a neurosurgical wound infection that has spread to cause meningitis. Cultures grow an ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, and a carbapenem is needed. His creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.2). The team must pick the carbapenem that best fits his central nervous system infection and seizure history.

Which carbapenem is the best choice?
choices: Imipenem-cilastatin at a high dose for better penetration
Ertapenem, because once-daily dosing reduces peak levels
Meropenem, preferred for CNS infections and less epileptogenic
Imipenem-cilastatin, since cilastatin prevents neurotoxicity
Aztreonam, the monobactam that avoids any carbapenem toxicity

explain.html:
Carbapenems are the drug of choice for serious ESBL infections. Among them, seizures and neurotoxicity are a class adverse effect with a clear ranking: imipenem greater than meropenem greater than ertapenem, and the risk is highest with impaired renal function, prior stroke, a history of seizures or high-dose imipenem. This patient has three of those risk factors.

The lecture's tip is that meropenem is preferred for CNS infections. Ertapenem has lower seizure risk but is the narrow carbapenem (no Pseudomonas) and causes hallucinations; it is not the CNS choice. Cilastatin protects imipenem from renal breakdown, not the brain.
why: High-dose imipenem with renal impairment and a seizure history carries the greatest seizure risk.
Ertapenem is not the preferred CNS carbapenem, and once-daily dosing is a convenience feature.
Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase; it does not prevent neurotoxicity.
ESBL enzymes hydrolyze aztreonam, so it would not work against this isolate.
explain.takeaway: Carbapenem seizure risk ranks imipenem over meropenem over ertapenem, highest with renal impairment or seizure history; meropenem is preferred for CNS infections.
explain.topic: Imipenem seizures and meropenem for CNS
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A research team studies a multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter isolate that has lost most of its outer membrane porins and overexpresses efflux pumps, so most beta-lactams never reach their targets. One cephalosporin still kills it. When the team grows the isolate in iron-rich medium, which shuts down bacterial iron uptake systems, that cephalosporin becomes much less effective.

Which mechanism best explains how this cephalosporin reaches its target?
choices: It chelates iron and rides the iron transport system across the outer membrane
It binds PBP2a, the altered target that blocks other beta-lactams
It is paired with a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects it in the periplasm
It inserts into the membrane with calcium and depolarizes the bacterial cell
It is small and polar enough to pass through the narrowed porin channels

explain.html:
This is cefiderocol, the siderophore cephalosporin. Its catechol group chelates ferric iron, and the complex is carried across the Gram-negative outer membrane by the bacterium's own active iron transport system, raising drug concentrations in the periplasm where PBPs sit. The lecture calls this a "Trojan horse" entry that bypasses porin loss and efflux resistance.

The iron-rich experiment confirms it: when bacteria do not need iron, they turn off the transporters, and the drug loses its way in. Cefiderocol covers multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, Enterobacterales and Stenotrophomonas.
why: PBP2a binding is ceftaroline against MRSA, a Gram-positive problem.
A beta-lactamase inhibitor would not explain the loss of activity in iron-rich medium.
Calcium-dependent membrane insertion is daptomycin, which has no Gram-negative activity.
Porin entry fails when porins are lost; that is exactly the barrier this drug bypasses.
explain.takeaway: Cefiderocol is a siderophore cephalosporin that chelates iron and enters Gram-negatives through iron transport channels, bypassing porin loss and efflux.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 59-year-old man is admitted with a perforated appendix and a pelvic abscess after a week of ventilator support for a prior surgery. The team wants one penicillin-based combination that covers enteric Gram-negative rods, the anaerobe Bacteroides fragilis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which was isolated from his sputum last week.

Which single agent provides all three kinds of coverage?
choices: Piperacillin-tazobactam
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Ampicillin-sulbactam
Nafcillin
Penicillin G

explain.html:
The lecture builds penicillin spectrum in blocks: natural penicillins cover streptococci; nafcillin adds MSSA; ampicillin and amoxicillin add Enterococcus and weak Gram-negative coverage; adding a beta-lactamase inhibitor (ampicillin-sulbactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate) adds MSSA, more Gram-negatives and anaerobes; and piperacillin-tazobactam adds Pseudomonas and the strongest Gram-negative activity.

Only piperacillin-tazobactam covers enteric Gram-negatives, B. fragilis and Pseudomonas together, which is why the lecture lists it for severe intra-abdominal infections and pseudomonal infections. Its tip: "Piperacillin/tazobactam equals Pseudomonas coverage."
why: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is oral, lacks Pseudomonas activity and is used for milder infections.
Ampicillin-sulbactam covers anaerobes and some Gram-negatives but not Pseudomonas.
Nafcillin is narrow, aimed at MSSA, with no Gram-negative or anaerobic coverage.
Penicillin G covers streptococci, Clostridium and Treponema, not these organisms.
explain.takeaway: Piperacillin-tazobactam is the penicillin combination that adds Pseudomonas to broad Gram-negative and anaerobic coverage, used for severe intra-abdominal and pseudomonal infections.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 68-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhea on day 6 of a hospital stay during which she received ceftriaxone. Stool testing is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin. She is started on vancomycin capsules by mouth. A medical student is surprised that serum vancomycin levels are not ordered, since the same drug given intravenously to another patient requires level monitoring and renal dose adjustment.

Which property of oral vancomycin best explains this difference?
choices: It is converted in the liver to an inactive metabolite before reaching blood
It binds calcium in the gut and forms an insoluble complex that is excreted
It is excreted entirely in bile, so renal function does not affect its levels
It is given at doses too low to cause toxicity, so levels are unnecessary
It has almost no systemic absorption, so it acts only within the gut lumen

explain.html:
The lecture is explicit: the oral formulation of vancomycin is for C. difficile infection only, because it has essentially zero systemic absorption. It stays in the colon, where the infection is, so it does not reach the blood, does not need serum levels and does not treat systemic infections.

Intravenous vancomycin, by contrast, distributes widely, is eliminated by the kidney and is nephrotoxic, so it requires renal dose adjustment and monitoring. The two routes are effectively two different drugs for two different jobs.
why: Vancomycin is not inactivated by hepatic metabolism; it simply is not absorbed from the gut.
Chelation with divalent cations is a tetracycline absorption problem, not the vancomycin story.
Biliary excretion is the ceftriaxone exception; vancomycin is renally eliminated when given intravenously.
Dose is not the reason; even large oral doses stay in the gut lumen.
explain.takeaway: Oral vancomycin is essentially unabsorbed and treats only C. difficile; intravenous vancomycin is renally cleared and nephrotoxic, requiring dose adjustment.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man has a painless, clean-based ulcer on the penis that appeared 3 weeks after unprotected intercourse, with firm, nontender inguinal nodes. Darkfield microscopy of the ulcer shows thin, motile spiral organisms. He has no drug allergies and receives a single intramuscular injection of the drug of choice. Four hours later he has a temperature of 39.0 C (102.2 F), chills, headache and diffuse myalgias. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and there is no rash, wheezing or swelling.

Which of the following best explains his new symptoms?
choices: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation triggered by the penicillin molecule
Release of bacterial products and a cytokine surge as the drug rapidly kills the spirochetes
Direct histamine release from mast cells caused by a rapid rate of drug delivery
Immune complex deposition one to two weeks after the drug binds serum proteins
Acute interstitial nephritis from a drug with a bulky beta-lactam side chain

explain.html:
The ulcer and spirochetes point to primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, and the lecture names penicillin G as the drug of choice. Fever, chills, headache and myalgias within hours of the first dose, with normal blood pressure and no urticaria or wheeze, is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, the adverse reaction the lecture links specifically to penicillin treatment of syphilis. It comes from products released by the rapidly dying organisms, not from allergy to the drug.

The distinction matters: a true IgE-mediated penicillin allergy would bring urticaria, wheezing or hypotension and would change future antibiotic choices, whereas this reaction is self-limited and does not mean he is allergic.
why: A true allergy would present with urticaria, bronchospasm or hypotension, none of which he has.
Rate-related direct histamine release with flushing is vancomycin flushing syndrome, after an infusion.
Serum sickness type reactions take days to weeks; this began within hours.
Interstitial nephritis is linked to nafcillin and presents with kidney injury, not a febrile reaction hours after a dose.
explain.takeaway: Penicillin G is the drug of choice for syphilis, and treatment can trigger the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, a febrile response to dying spirochetes rather than an allergy.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man with a skin abscess develops bacteremia. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are susceptible to oxacillin. He is started on the drug of choice for this organism given intravenously. On day 12 he develops a diffuse maculopapular rash and low-grade fever.

Creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9; normal 0.6 to 1.2)
Eosinophils (blood): 9% (normal 1 to 4)
Urinalysis: white blood cells and white cell casts; no bacteria

Which drug most likely caused this complication?
choices: Vancomycin
Cefazolin
Nafcillin
Ceftriaxone
Ampicillin

explain.html:
Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are oxacillin susceptible are methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). The lecture calls the anti-staphylococcal penicillins (nafcillin, oxacillin) the drug of choice for MSSA, because their bulky side chains resist staphylococcal beta-lactamase.

Rash, fever, eosinophilia, rising creatinine and white cell casts after more than a week of therapy describe acute interstitial nephritis, which the lecture assigns to nafcillin more than oxacillin. Oxacillin, by contrast, leans toward hepatitis and hyperbilirubinemia. Vancomycin is nephrotoxic too, but it is not the drug of choice for MSSA and its kidney injury is not an eosinophilic, allergic-type nephritis.
why: Vancomycin covers MSSA but is not its drug of choice, and its nephrotoxicity is not the rash-plus-eosinophilia picture.
Cefazolin treats MSSA bacteremia and is described as well tolerated, without a nephritis signature.
Ceftriaxone is not the MSSA drug of choice, and its signature effects are biliary sludging and hyperbilirubinemia.
Ampicillin is not reliable against beta-lactamase-producing staphylococci.
explain.takeaway: Nafcillin is the drug of choice for MSSA infections and is the beta-lactam most associated with acute interstitial nephritis (oxacillin with hepatotoxicity).
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 9-day-old boy is brought in for poor feeding, irritability and a temperature of 38.9 C (102 F). Lumbar puncture shows a cerebrospinal fluid white cell count of 1,800/microL (normal under 30) with neutrophil predominance and low glucose. Gram stain shows short Gram-positive rods. Empiric therapy is started with cefotaxime plus a second agent, because the cephalosporin alone would leave the likely organism uncovered.

Which second agent is added, and why?
choices: Vancomycin, because the organism has altered penicillin-binding protein 2a
Gentamicin alone, because it reaches high concentrations in the CSF
Aztreonam, because the organism is a Gram-positive that lacks a cell wall
Metronidazole, because the organism is an obligate anaerobic spore former
Ampicillin, because cephalosporins do not reliably cover this rod

explain.html:
Short Gram-positive rods causing neonatal meningitis point to Listeria monocytogenes. The lecture names ampicillin as the drug of choice for Listeria meningitis ("Amp up for Listeria") and lists cefotaxime for neonatal meningitis, often given with ampicillin. The reason for the pairing is that cephalosporins do not reliably cover Listeria (or Enterococcus), so the ampicillin fills that gap.

Ampicillin also penetrates the CSF, which the lecture lists among the penicillin pharmacokinetic facts (penicillin, ampicillin and nafcillin reach the CSF).
why: PBP2a is the MRSA resistance target; vancomycin is not the agent added for Listeria.
Aminoglycosides are not used alone for Gram-positive organisms; their Gram-positive role is synergy with a cell wall agent.
Aztreonam has no Gram-positive activity at all, and Listeria has a cell wall.
Listeria is not an anaerobic spore former, and metronidazole is for anaerobes and protozoa.
explain.takeaway: Ampicillin is the drug of choice for Listeria meningitis and is added to a cephalosporin for neonatal meningitis because cephalosporins do not cover Listeria.
explain.topic: Ampicillin for Listeria and neonatal meningitis
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 5-day-old girl born at 36 weeks is evaluated for fever. She has visible jaundice, with total bilirubin of 14 mg/dL (high for age), and she is receiving intravenous fluids that contain calcium. The resident suggests a third-generation cephalosporin that is given once daily, is excreted mainly in bile and is known for causing biliary sludging in adults. The pharmacist recommends a different agent.

What is the main reason to avoid the suggested drug in this patient?
choices: It accumulates dangerously in kidneys that are still immature in a newborn
It worsens hyperbilirubinemia and can precipitate with intravenous calcium
It causes seizures in neonates by antagonizing GABA receptors in the brain
It fails to reach the cerebrospinal fluid if the fever is caused by meningitis
It causes a disulfiram-like reaction with the alcohol in neonatal preparations

explain.html:
The drug described is ceftriaxone: third generation, biliary excretion (the exception among cephalosporins, which makes it safe in renal failure) and biliary sludging. The lecture lists its unique adverse effects as hyperbilirubinemia and neonatal jaundice, which make it contraindicated in neonates, and calcium binding with precipitation, a concern for intravenous compatibility.

This jaundiced newborn on calcium-containing fluids has both problems. Cefotaxime is the third-generation agent the lecture uses for neonatal meningitis instead.
why: Ceftriaxone is cleared mainly in bile, so renal accumulation is not the concern.
Seizures and encephalopathy are linked to cefepime (and imipenem), not ceftriaxone.
Ceftriaxone does penetrate the CSF; that is why it is used for meningitis in older patients.
A disulfiram-like reaction is linked to cefotetan (and metronidazole), not ceftriaxone.
explain.takeaway: Ceftriaxone is excreted in bile, can cause biliary sludging and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and precipitates with calcium, so it is avoided in neonates (cefotaxime is used instead).
explain.topic: Ceftriaxone in neonates and biliary excretion
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 3.1 mg/dL; normal 0.6 to 1.2) is admitted with febrile neutropenia during chemotherapy. She is started on the fourth-generation cephalosporin that covers staphylococci, streptococci, Enterobacter and Pseudomonas, at a full dose not adjusted for her kidney function. On day 4 she becomes confused and has myoclonic jerks, and an electroencephalogram shows epileptiform discharges. Brain imaging is normal.

Which of the following best explains her neurologic findings?
choices: Bacterial meningitis caused by Pseudomonas that the drug failed to cover
Serotonin syndrome from weak monoamine oxidase inhibition by the drug
Hepatic encephalopathy from cholestatic injury caused by the drug
Drug accumulation causing neurotoxicity with encephalopathy
Hypocalcemia from calcium precipitation with the drug in the plasma

explain.html:
The drug is cefepime, the fourth-generation cephalosporin the lecture uses for febrile neutropenia and broad empiric coverage including Pseudomonas. Cephalosporins are excreted mainly unchanged by the kidney, so an unadjusted dose in severe kidney disease accumulates.

The lecture lists neurotoxicity (encephalopathy and seizures, especially in renal failure or at higher doses) as cefepime's signature adverse effect, which fits her confusion, myoclonus and epileptiform EEG with normal imaging.
why: Cefepime does cover Pseudomonas and penetrates CSF; the picture fits drug toxicity, not a missed organism.
Weak MAO inhibition and serotonin syndrome belong to linezolid, not cefepime.
Cefepime is not associated with cholestatic liver injury; hyperbilirubinemia is a ceftriaxone feature.
Calcium precipitation is a ceftriaxone compatibility problem, not a cause of this syndrome.
explain.takeaway: Cefepime, the fourth-generation anti-pseudomonal cephalosporin, causes encephalopathy and seizures, especially when not dose-adjusted in renal failure.
explain.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem:
A 54-year-old man has a Pseudomonas aeruginosa urinary tract infection with bacteremia. His record notes two prior reactions: hives and throat swelling after amoxicillin 10 years ago, and generalized urticaria with hypotension during an infusion of ceftazidime last year. The team considers a beta-lactam with a single, unfused ring that covers only Gram-negative organisms, including Pseudomonas.

Which statement best describes the safety of that drug for this patient?
choices: It is a concern, because it shares a side chain with ceftazidime
It is unsafe, because it shares the amoxicillin side chain and cross-reacts
It is safe, because it has no cross-reactivity with any other beta-lactam
It is safe, because its reactions are histamine release and not IgE mediated
It is unsafe, because all beta-lactams share the same immunogenic ring

explain.html:
The drug is aztreonam, the monobactam: a monocyclic beta-lactam ring, Gram-negative only ("A Z for zero Gram-positive, zero anaerobes"). Because the immune system does not recognize it as a penicillin or cephalosporin, it is the option for serious Gram-negative infections in patients with true IgE-mediated beta-lactam allergy, and it has no cross-reactivity with penicillins.

The lecture flags one exception: aztreonam cross-reacts with ceftazidime (and probably cefiderocol) because they share a similar side chain. This patient's amoxicillin anaphylaxis would not rule aztreonam out, but his ceftazidime reaction does make it a real concern. Cross-reactivity follows side chains, not the beta-lactam ring itself.
why: Aztreonam has no cross-reactivity with penicillins such as amoxicillin.
Aztreonam does cross-react with ceftazidime, so "no cross-reactivity with any beta-lactam" is too broad.
His reactions were urticaria with hypotension and throat swelling, which are IgE-type, and histamine release describes vancomycin.
Cross-reactivity depends on side chains, not on a shared beta-lactam ring.
explain.takeaway: Aztreonam does not cross-react with penicillins and is used in true beta-lactam allergy, but it can cross-react with ceftazidime because of a shared side chain.

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man with a prosthetic knee infection grows Gram-positive cocci in clusters resistant to oxacillin. Ten minutes into a rapid intravenous infusion of the first-line drug for this organism, he develops intense flushing and itching of the face, neck and upper chest. Blood pressure falls from 128/80 to 102/64 mm Hg. He has no wheezing, lip swelling or urticarial wheals. He has tolerated this same drug before when it was infused over 2 hours.

Which is the most appropriate next step?
choices: Record a permanent allergy and switch to a beta-lactam for the infection
Stop the drug and give epinephrine, then switch to daptomycin for life
Give an antihistamine and restart it at a slower infusion rate
Add an aminoglycoside so that a lower dose of the drug can be infused
Switch to the oral form of the drug, which avoids this infusion reaction

explain.html:
Oxacillin-resistant staphylococci are MRSA, and the first-line drug is vancomycin. Flushing and itching over the upper chest, neck and face, with mild hypotension, during a fast infusion is vancomycin flushing (infusion) syndrome. The lecture stresses that it is histamine mediated, related to the rate of infusion and not a true allergy, so it is managed with antihistamines and a longer infusion time.

Labeling it an allergy would wrongly remove a key MRSA drug, and switching to a beta-lactam would fail against MRSA. Oral vancomycin is essentially not absorbed and is used only for C. difficile, so it cannot treat a joint infection.
why: This is not a true allergy, and standard beta-lactams do not treat MRSA.
Epinephrine and permanent avoidance fit anaphylaxis, which this rate-related histamine reaction is not.
Adding an aminoglycoside does not address an infusion-rate reaction and adds nephrotoxicity.
Oral vancomycin has nearly zero systemic absorption and treats only C. difficile.
explain.takeaway: Vancomycin flushing syndrome is a rate-related, histamine-mediated reaction (not an allergy) managed with antihistamines and a slower infusion.
